name: Ampass
kurzbeschreibung: Peaceful village at the entrance to the Stubaital, featuring a Gothic parish church and beautiful hiking trails into the surrounding forests.
beschreibung:
Overview

Ampass is situated at an elevation of 651 meters on a sunny plateau of the southeastern low mountain terrace approximately eight kilometers southeast of Innsbruck, perched above the Inn Valley between Amras and the historic town of Hall in Tirol. Located in the district of Innsbruck-Land, the municipality covers an area of roughly eight square kilometers with around 1,900 residents. The elevated terrace offers commanding panoramic views across the Inn Valley, the Nordkette mountain chain, and Mount Patscherkofel. Despite its close proximity to Innsbruck, Ampass has preserved the peaceful charm of an authentic Tyrolean village with traditional farmsteads, orchards, and woodland trails.

History

Ampass is one of the oldest settled locations in North Tyrol, with archaeological artifacts dating back to the Bronze Age. The Demlfeld site was home to a major Iron Age sacrificial altar, and Roman salt and trade routes crossed the area toward the Brenner Pass. The village was first documented in 1145 as Ambans, a Celtic name meaning 'between two streams'. Following the destruction of Ambras Castle chapel in the 12th century, the parish seat moved to Ampass and was incorporated into Wilten Abbey in 1256. The village endured trials including wartime sacking in 1546, a devastating fire in 1567, and powerful earthquakes in 1670 and 1689.

Getting There

Reaching Ampass by public transit is swift: VVT regional bus line 4134 runs frequently from Innsbruck Central Station and Hall in Tirol railway station, reaching the village center in 15 to 20 minutes. For motorists, the village is conveniently accessed via the Inntal Motorway A12 via exits Innsbruck-Ost or Hall-West, connecting via the L283 Ampass regional road in five to ten minutes. A toll-free scenic route connects directly from Innsbruck through Amras. Cyclists can ascend to the plateau via regional cycling routes connecting from the Inn Valley Cycle Path.

Tips

The town's preeminent landmark is the Parish Church of Saint John the Baptist on the Sonnenbichl hill, featuring a detached bell tower, Gothic masonry, magnificent 1744 Rococo stuccowork, and the historic 1717 bell 'Ampigerin'—making it one of Tyrol's most cherished wedding churches. Another cultural treasure is the late-Gothic Viertelsäule wayside plague column from the late 15th century, immortalized on the town's coat of arms. The Gothic Saint Vitus Church on the Veitsbühel dates to 1429, built by salt trade carters. Pilgrims and hikers can follow the Tyrolean Camino de Santiago crossing through town, or hike scenic trails toward Glungezer and Sistrans.
